chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Rifa'ah ibn Musa who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mahrud (one with a defect) and the Mahrudah (female with a defect), is she returned from the marriage? He said: No.

Rifa'ah said: And I asked him about the Brasa' (woman with leprosy/white patches), so he said: The Commander of the Faithful ruled regarding a woman whom her guardian married while she was Brasa', that she has the Mahr (dowry) because he made lawful her private part, and that the Mahr is upon the one who married her, and the Mahr became upon him because he concealed her defect. And if a man married a woman, or a man married her off, who did not know the inner nature of her affair (defect), there would be nothing upon him, and he would take the Mahr from her.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on marriage with a physically defective spouse regarding the dowry (Mahr)?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies that a physical defect (Mahrudah) does not automatically invalidate marriage or require the woman to be 'returned,' but rather governs the financial compensation (Mahr) based on the principle of concealment (Tadlis). Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the husband's right to retain Mahr if the defect was known or not actively hidden by the wali, versus the wali's liability if he concealed it, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on fairness in marital contracts. This ruling underscores the importance of transparency in marriage negotiations and the specific liability of the contracting party rather than the spouse herself.
